headline: Deputy asks Commission if 260,000 public staff may campaign in 2027
dek: The Election Commission's calendar fixes dates but says nothing on staff conduct; its chairman promises guidance before nominations open on 1 June.
paragraphs: Mejlis deputy Kseniya Shubina has written to the Territorial Election Commission asking whether public employees, among them teachers, clinic staff and city and district clerks, may take part in campaigning for a ticket, or be asked to speak for one at work, and what protects them if they decline. The election is on 2 November 2027, a little under a year away.

The question covers a large share of the workforce. Of the roughly 690,000 formal jobs in the ISEZ, about 260,000 are in the public sector and state enterprises, or about 38 per cent, according to the figures the Ministry of Economy uses for its labour planning. Whatever the Commission answers will reach more than a third of those in regular employment.

Commission chairman Daniyar Borubaev replied that the preliminary calendar, Decision 2026/4 of 30 September, sets dates but does not deal with staff conduct. Register revision begins on 1 March 2027, nominations run from 1 June to 2 August, the campaign starts on 1 October and certification is due by 12 November. Mr Borubaev said the Commission's guidance for the 2027 campaign will be published "before nominations open on 1 June". He named no content and did not say whether staff conduct will be in it.

Ms Shubina, who directed a Russian-language school in Nurzhan from 1998 to 2011 and sits for the Nurzhan city constituency on a civic list, said the letter came from constituents rather than from a particular incident. "A teacher should know on the first of September what she may be asked on the first of October," she said. She asked that the answer be written down and published, not given orally to individual directors.

The Teachers' and Educators' Union, which has about 38,000 members, welcomed the request. Its chair, Rahat Osmon kyzy, said clarity is a reasonable thing to ask for. "The union does not choose candidates," she said. "Our members want to know where the line is, and who they can ask."

In Nurzhan, Galina Pavlenko, who teaches history at a city school, said nobody has asked her for anything. "But nobody has told me I can say no, either," she said. Tynchtyk Orozaliev, a clerk at a Chu District office, said much the same: he would like the rules in writing before the summer, so that a supervisor and a clerk are reading the same page.

Dr Aruuke Jakypova, a political scientist at the TSU Institute of Sociology, said the gap is not unusual in a calendar that is still preliminary, but that the timing matters. Staff who will be asked to staff polling stations, collect signatures or attend meetings will plan their autumn long before 1 June. A rule that appears after nominations open, she said, would reach them after habits are set.

The Ministry of Education and the Ministry of Health, which between them employ most of the teachers and clinic staff in question, gave no comment. The Commission has not said whether it will consult the ministries or the unions on its guidance, or whether a draft will be published for comment first.

Ms Shubina said she will ask the Mejlis's relevant committee to put the Commission's reply on its record. The next fixed date is 1 March 2027, when register revision begins; the guidance is due before 1 June.
